name: Quartz-Eternal
description: Quartz-Eternal is a tidally locked ice world whose sunward hemisphere is a dazzling field of quartz-infused ice that catches the permanent daylight in a million facets, while the dark side plunges into temperatures that freeze methane into solid lakes. The transition zone hosts crystal caverns of staggering beauty, where thermal gradients have grown quartz formations over millions of years into structures that resemble frozen cathedrals. A subterranean ocean circulates beneath both hemispheres, warmed by a fading geothermal source.

Time feels different on Quartz-Eternal, and not only subjectively. Temporal distortion zones have been measured in the deepest crystal caverns, micro-regions where atomic clocks drift at rates inconsistent with relativistic predictions. The effect is small but real, and standing in the caverns produces a disorienting sense of temporal dislocation, a feeling of being unstuck from the present moment. The quartz formations amplify and focus ambient light into concentrated beams that sweep the cavern interiors like slow searchlights.

The subterranean ocean hosts microbial life that metabolizes exotic matter trace elements, organisms whose biochemistry operates at the boundary of understood physics. These microbes are endangered by the planet's cooling core, as the geothermal energy that sustains the liquid ocean is measurably diminishing. In geological terms, the ocean will freeze solid within a few million years, ending the last life on the planet.

Quartz-Eternal's temporal anomalies have drawn theoretical physicists from across settled space, and the exotic matter microbes are of intense interest to multiple research institutions. The planet's slow death adds urgency to the study, a clock running down on phenomena that may not exist anywhere else. The crystal caverns are hauntingly beautiful, and those who spend time in the distortion zones report a persistent sense of loss, as though they have glimpsed something precious that is already slipping away.
